idiom_name: same-type operation on an immutable value type (combine(Value, Value) -> Value)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: fix the canonical representation, expose construction only through validating factories, then give the type operations whose parameters and result are the type itself. Keep the type immutable - every operation returns a fresh instance built from the canonical representation and re-establishes the invariant (unit or currency compatibility, bounds, normalisation) before returning; never hand back a primitive, a tuple of fields or a foreign concept where the type would do. Name the operations in the domain's language (add, subtract, union, intersect, append, extend), and when an operation is only half-closed (a scalar factor, a comparison, a projection) or can fail, give it a distinct signature and name instead of faking closure. The algebraic classification matters: if the operation is associative with an identity, the type is a monoid; if only associative, it is a semigroup; if neither law holds, it is a magma (Seemann, 2017). Test the algebraic laws explicitly.
code_sketch:
def combine(a: Value, b: Value) -> Value:        # arguments and result: same type
    require_compatible(a, b)                      # unit / currency / bounds invariant
    return Value.from_canonical(canonical(a) + canonical(b))

def zero() -> Value: ...                          # identity, only if the domain has one

total = reduce(combine, values, zero())           # folds stay inside the type
pitfalls: Skipping the invariant check inside the operation pushes it back to call sites, which is exactly the coupling the pattern removes.
Returning a primitive or a tuple from the 'combination' leaves the type half-closed and forces every caller to reconstruct an instance.
Inventing an identity element (an 'empty' or 'zero' value the domain does not have) so that generic folds type-check.
Naming a closed operation with a verb that does not obey the algebraic laws its name implies (e.g., calling a non-associative operation 'add').
Using operator overloading for operations that are not arithmetic in nature, making the call site misleading.

Wrong move: apply closure as a universal interface rule so every method becomes same-type -> failure: queries and comparisons get contorted into wrapper values, the abstraction degenerates into 'closure fever' with an anemic vocabulary no domain expert recognises -> instead: treat closure as a heuristic for genuinely combining operations and leave queries and projections honestly open.

Wrong move: wire a closed operation into a reduce or parallel fold without testing the laws -> failure: a non-associative combination or a fabricated identity yields order-dependent totals, which the JDK reduce contract explicitly forbids -> instead: verify associativity and identity by property test first, and use the Optional fold form when the domain has no identity.

Wrong move: return a magic same-type value (empty interval, zero money) for a partial operation so the signature looks fully closed -> failure: callers cannot distinguish 'no common part' from a legitimate empty result and the sentinel leaks into business rules -> instead: model absence explicitly in the type system - Joda-Time's overlap() and NodaTime's Union/Intersection return null/Option rather than invent an interval.
sources: Mark Seemann, 'Monoids, Semigroups, and Friends', ploeh.dk, 2017 — connects closure of operations to monoids, semigroups, and magmas from abstract algebra.
Arolla, 'Domain Modeling with Monoids', 2018 PDF — monoid patterns in domain modeling, configuration composition, supply chain aggregation.
Scott Wlaschin, 'Domain Modeling Made Functional' — F# functional DDD, value objects, and composable domain types.
Herberto Graca, 'DDD 10 – Supple Design', herbertograca.com, 2015 — commentary on Evans' supple design patterns.
